div.p: Supravital species identification of morphologically similar syntopic earthworms inhabiting dung and compost heaps or those from commercial cultures is difficult. The aim of the studies was to find out non-invasive species-specific markers for proper segregation of earthworm species from a dense mixed colony of waste decomposers. Worms were segregated according to external characteristics into Eisenia andrei, Eisenia fetida, and Dendrobaena veneta, and left for reproduction and analysis of non-invasively retrieved coelomocyte-containing coelomic fluid and/ or species-specific partial sequences of cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) gene in DNA extracted from amputated tail tips of adults and their offspring. Flow cytometric analysis of coelomocyte samples revealed that amount of nuclear DNA increases in order D. veneta ( E. andrei < E. fetida, and intensity of eleocyte-derived fluorescence is lower in D. veneta than in Eisenia spp. Spectrofluorimetry of coelomocyte lysates revealed that the amount of eleocyte-stored riboflavin is significantly lower in coelomocyte lysates from D. veneta than from Eisenia spp., and the emission peak of X-fluorophore is much more distinct in D. veneta than in Eisenia spp. Coelomic fluid of E. andrei exhibits a very distinct spectra of MUG fluorophore which are absent in D. veneta and in the majority of E. fetida, while some E. fetida possess MUG-like fluorophore. Sequences of the COI gene in the DNA of the worms from the mixed colony and their offspring confirmed species identity. In conclusion, species-specific coelomocyte-derived markers may be a useful complement to morphological and DNA-based taxonomy during studies on syntopic earthworms.

Some epigeic earthworm species, like Eisenia spp. and Dendrobaena veneta are adapted to decaying organic material, therefore they often live in mixed colonies in dung and compost heaps or they are commercially cultured for the vermicomposting and fish bait market. They are also often used as convenient models in several scientific disciplines including ecotoxicology (e.g., Brulle et al., 2006Brulle et al., , 2008Brulle et al., , 2011) ) and immunology (Bilej et al., 2011;Rorat et al., 2013), where accurate identification of test organisms is of critical importance. For scientific purposes the composting worms may be either field-collected or bought from commercial suppliers, but in both instances we may obtain rather a mixture of several species than a pure culture of one of them. It is difficult to segregate them, especially juvenile specimens, according to external examination of living specimens. Traditional methods in earthworm taxonomy rely on morphological criteria based on observation of the formalin-or alcohol-fixed adult specimens exhibiting a clitellum, with special attention to the details visible under a dissecting microscope, especially those concerning the numbers and arrangements of setae, details of prostomium, location of tubercula pubertalis, and genital tumescence (e.g., Kasprzak,'86;Sims and Gerard,'85).

Earthworm identification is especially difficult in the case of Eisenia fetida/andrei complex of morphologically similar syntopic species termed indiscriminately as E. fetida (or E. foetida), which live in mixed colonies in dung and compost heaps. They were originally described as different morphotypes of E. fetida according to differences in body pigmentation, and Andre ('63) named the striped ("brandling," "tiger") form E. fetida var. typica and the "red" form E. fetida var. unicolor. Then Bouche ('72) gave them sub-species status, naming them E. fetida fetida and E. fetida andrei, but Dominguez et al. (2005) evidenced the existence of reproductive isolation between them, proving that they can be considered distinct biological species, Eisenia fetida (Savigny) and Eisenia andrei (Bouche). Most recently, the DNA barcoding provided a method to accurately identify E. fetida and E. andrei from free-living populations (Pérez-Losada et al., 2005) and laboratory colonies (Otomo et al., 2009).

The use of DNA barcodes, which are short sequences from standardized regions of genome, is a powerful tool and a useful complement to traditional morphological taxonomy of various earthworm species (e.g., Huang et al., 2007;Pérez-Losada et al., 2009). This method revealed unprecedented diversity of the morphologically identical cryptic species within lumbricid earthworms (King et al., 2008), which can be distinguished only by analysis of some conserved DNA sequences, among them the mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase I (COI) gene (King et al., 2008;Otomo et al., 2009;Klarica et al., 2012). The DNA samples for species identification may be extracted either from amputated and alcohol-fixed caudal segments (e.g., Plytycz et al., 2009;Klarica et al., 2012) or from non-invasively extruded coelomocytes (e.g., Brulle et al., 2006;Homa et al., 2010), allowing supravital identification of specimens.

DNA-based species identification provides a means to identify not only adults but also juvenile earthworms but is still rather expensive and time consuming. Therefore it is reasonable to search for other molecular markers derived from non-invasively retrieved coelomocytes, which can be extruded by dorsal pores of earthworms irritated by mild electrostimulation (Roch,'79), immersion in 5% ethanol (Cooper et al.,'95), or ultrasounds (Hendawi et al., 2004).

The coelomocytes are the main cellular components of the earthworm innate immunity (Bilej et al., 2011). Composting species are exposed to a large diversity of microorganisms, thus their immune system is strongly challenged by microbial antigens and various sorts of pollutants and has to be very efficient to cope with them successfully (e.g., Rorat et al., 2013). Among coelomocytes floating within the earthworm coelomic cavity, there are amebocytes (being classical immunocytes according to Ottaviani, 2011) and species-specific numbers of chloragogenous tissue-derived autofluorescent eleocytes. Autofluorescence selfmarking made them an ideal object of flow cytometric analysis (Cholewa et al., 2006), fluorescence and confocal microscopic observations (Plytycz et al., 2007) and spectrofluorimetric measurements (Koziol et al., 2006). The latter method revealed that the riboflavin (i.e., vitamin B2-a potent immunomodulatory agent) is one of the fluorophores stored in chloragosomes of chloragocytes and chloragocyte-derived eleocytes (Koziol et al., 2006). Its amount is species-specific (Plytycz et al., 2006) and changes in response to various edaphic factors, including heavy metal pollution (Plytycz et al., 2009(Plytycz et al., , 2011a,b;,b;Plytycz and Morgan, 2011). Eleocytes of some species (e.g., E. fetida) accumulate high amounts of riboflavin in chloragosomes, while the amount of riboflavin is low in D. veneta, despite the intensive autofluorescence of eleocytes of this species, which putatively derives mainly from lipofuscin (Cygal et al., 2007). There are also lumbricid species (e.g., Lumbricus terrestris or Aporrectodea caliginosa) without eleocytes in coelomic fluid (Cholewa et al., 2006), but riboflavin is stored in chloragocytes of their chloragogenous tissue (Mazur et al., 2011). These results show that autofluorescent eleocytes and riboflavin content in coelomocyte samples, non-invasively retrieved from the coelom, belong to molecular supravital markers specific for some earthworm species (Plytycz et al., 2006;Plytycz and Morgan, 2011). Other speciesspecific fluorescence markers were discovered by Albani et al. (2003) in Eisenia spp.

The aim of the studies is to apply molecular markers derived from non-invasively retrieved coelomocyte-containing coelomic fluid, that is, the amount of nuclear DNA in coelomocyte samples and species-specific contents of coelomocyte-derived fluorophores, verified by the DNA barcoding, for supravital segregation of morphologically similar syntopic oligochaetes, that is, specimens of E. andrei, E. fetida, and D. veneta from the mixed colony of composting earthworms.

div.head: Earthworms
div.p: Adult composting earthworms were kindly provided from the wastewater treatment plant in Kluczbork in October 2011 and reared in the laboratory of Institute of Zoology, Jagiellonian University in Krakow, under controlled conditions (17 AE 2°C; 12:12 LD, 50% humidity) in plastic boxes with perforated lids in the soil from the commercial supplier (PPUH BIOVITA, Tenczynek, Poland). Adults E. andrei and E. fetida were delivered from genetically defined colonies maintained within Lille University (France). D. veneta reared in Krakow laboratory originated from the commercial supplier (Ekagro, Kepa Slupska, Poland). In Krakow laboratory, worms were fed ad libitum on a mixed diet comprised of flour, boiled/dried/powdered tea leaves, nettle and dandelion leaves, and powdered mouse feed.

div.head: Experimental Scheme
div.p: Worms provided from Kluczbork consisted in a dense stock culture of animals of similar body size not exceeding 1 g body weight. Adult earthworms of similar body weights (mean þ SD ¼ 0.72 þ 0.14 g) with well-developed clitellum were selected and preliminarily segregated according to morphological criteria into E. fetida, E. andrei, and D. veneta (Fig. 1A-C). Ten animals per species were kept in fresh soil in separate boxes. Each worm was tested at the beginning and the end of a 5-week experimental period. Adults, cocoons, and juveniles of segregated species were cultured further for reproduction and future analyses. Eisenia spp. from Lille and D. veneta from Krakow served as additional controls of species identification.

Earthworms were used for non-invasive retrieval of coelomocyte containing coelomic fluid which served for spetrofluorimetric detection of fluorophores and/or for flow-cytometric detection of DNA profiles/amount. Before testing, each worm was kept individually in a separate enumerated box with a perforated lid filled with wet filter papers. After coelomocyte extrusion followed by 1-day isolation (for analysis of coelomocytes and fluorophores) worms with the confirmed identity (D. veneta, E. andrei, E. fetida) were put into fresh soil again and kept for reproduction. The offspring of these earthworms were tested individually in respect of coelomic fluid-derived factors, while their tail tips (3-4 caudal segments fixed in 70% ethanol) were used for genotyping. Analysis of fluorophores and DNA amounts in coelomocyte lysates were also performed in specimens of E. andrei and E. fetida from genetically defined colonies raised in Lille and D. veneta from Kraków.

div.head: Harvesting Coelomocytes
div.p: Earthworms were stimulated for 30 sec with a 4.5 V electric current to expel coelomic fluid with suspended coelomocytes through the dorsal pores, as described previously (Plytycz et al., 2006). Briefly, earthworms were placed individually in Petri dishes containing 3 mL of extrusion fluid (phosphate-buffered saline, PBS, supplemented with 2.5 g/L ethylenediamine tetra-acetic acid, EDTA). Freshly prepared 2 mL suspensions were used for spectrofluorimetry and the remaining sample from each worm was fixed in 70% alcohol (for cell cycle/DNA amount) or in 2% formalin for coelomocyte counting in hemocytometer and for flow cytometry detection of autofluorescent elocytes.

div.head: Flow Cytometric Measurements and Analysis
div.p: Percentages of Autofluorescent Eleocytes. Samples of coelomocytes were analyzed with a FACScalibur flow cytometer (Beckton-Dickinson, San Jose, CA, USA). During analytical experiments, 5,000 threshold events per worm sample were collected and analyzed on the basis of their forward scatter (FS) (for cell size) and sideward scatter (SS) (cell complexity) properties. Fluorescence FL1-H (emission 530 nm; excitation 488 nm) was recorded. The resulting files were analyzed using WinMDI 2.8 software (Joe Trotter, http://facs.scripps.edu), by producing dot plots of cell size versus FL1 autofluorescence.

DNA Amounts. For estimation of DNA amounts according to modified protocol originally developed by Birstein et al. ('93), freshly retrieved coelomocytes were washed in PBS, fixed in icecold 70% ethanol and kept in À20°C for 2 hr or overnight. Afterwards cells adjusted to 10 6 cells/mL were washed with 0.2% Triton-X (Sigma-Aldrich, Saint Louis, MO, USA) in PBS and stained with propidium iodide (PI, Sigma, 50 mg/mL) in 0.1% sodium citrate (Sigma-Aldrich) containing 10 ng/mL RNase A (Sigma-Aldrich). Then, cells were incubated for 30 min in the dark and analyzed on LSR II with Diva software (BD Biosciences). 10,000 events from each sample were collected in the single cell gate created on the PE-W (transit time) versus PE-A (total cell fluorescence) cytogram to exclude aggregates and debris from the analyses. Autofluorescent cells based on a FITC-PE dot plot were also excluded from the analysis, as their fluorescence interferes with the signal from PI. Median fluorescence of cells in G1 phase was used for estimation of the DNA content. As a reference of the PI staining served the cell cycle profiles of U937 human monocytic cell line cultured routinely in the Department of Medical Biotechnology, Faculty of Biochemistry, Biophysics, and Biotechnology, Jagiellonian University and/or chicken red blood cells (CRBC) kindly provided by Dr. M. Lis from the University of Agriculture, Krakow, Poland.

div.head: Spectrofluorimetric Measurements and Analysis
div.p: Spectrofluorimetric measurements were performed using Perkin-Elmer Spectrofluorimeter LS50B. Samples of the extruded coelomocyte-containing coelomic fluids were initially centrifuged at 7,500g for 30 min at 4°C, and supernatants were used for spectrofluorimetry according to Koziol et al. (2006) and Albani et al. (2003). We modified the procedure applied previously for riboflavin detection (see Plytycz et al., 2006), that is, 1 mL of coelomocyte-containing coelomic fluid was lysed in 0.2% Triton X (Sigma-Aldrich) (20 min) and then the solution was diluted with 1 mL PBS to the volume of 2 mL required for spectrofluorimeter cuvettes. As both of the procedures gave almost identical results concerning riboflavin, and Triton-lysed samples gave additional information concerning the X-fluorophore, majority of samples were analyzed using Triton lysates as simpler, faster for handling, and delivering more information. MUG Fluorophore. MUG fluorophore was detected by a modified method originally described by Albani et al. (2003). As in a paper by Albani et al. (2003), emission spectra of MUG-like fluorophore were recorded between 340 and 480 nm (lambda at 320 nm) while excitation spectra were recorded between 260 and 360 nm (lambda at 380).

Riboflavin. Riboflavin emission spectra were recorded between 400 and 680 nm (lambda at 370 nm) while excitation spectra were recorded between 300 and 510 nm (lambda at 525 nm) (Plytycz et al., 2006).

DNA Analysis DNA Isolation. Earthworms' tails were cut and kept in 70% alcohol and transported to University of Lille Nord de France, LGCgE. DNA was isolated using standard protocol for NucleoSpin® Tissue kit (Macherey-Nagel, Düren, Germany). DNA purity was determined using spectrophotometry (BioPhotometer, Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany) and in all analyzed samples A260/A80 ratio was in range 1.8-2.0. DNA Amplification. Thermal cycling was done in 0.2 mL thin walled PCR tubes with: 1 mL template (DNA extracted as described above), 1 mL of 10 mM primers for amplification of the 5 0 side of the mitochondrial DNA cytochrome oxidase subunit I (COI) region (LCO1490: 5 0 -GGTCAACAAATCATAAAGATATTGG-3 0 , HCO2198: 5 0 -TAAACTTCAGGGTGACCAAAAAATCA-3 0 ; Folmer et al., '94), 5 mL 5Â Green GoTaq Flexi buffer, 0.5 mL dNTPs (10 mM each), 0.2 mL GoTaq polymerase and nuclease free water to 25 mL. PCR cycling conditions were an initial denaturation step of 94°C for 5 min followed by 45 cycles of 94°C for 30 sec, 50°C for 30 sec, 72°C

for 1 min, and a final extension to 72°C for 5 min. Six microliters of each PCR reaction were verified on 1% agarose gel stained with ethidium bromide. The remaining volume of reaction was sent to the Genoscreen Company (Lille, France) for purification and direct Sanger sequencing in one direction with forward primer LCO1490.

COI sequences provided by Genoscreen Company were corrected using Chromas (Technelysium Pty. Ltd., South Brisbane, Australia). All earthworms sequences generated in this study were deposited in GenBank (KC788574-KC88619).

Data Analysis. E. fetida (AY874513-16), E. andrei (AY874494, AY874499, AY874504, AY874508, DQ914619-21, DQ914627), and D. veneta (FJ214233, FJ214238) sequences from Genbank and previous studies (Pérez-Losada et al., 2005, Otomo et al., 2009) were aligned to the sequences generated in this study (KC788574-KC88619) using Muscle under the default settings on the web service www.phylogeny.fr (Dereeper et al., 2008). A phylogeny tree using maximum likelihood was constructed in PhyML 3.0 aLRT with HKY85 model, and SH-like statistical test, under the default substitution model. The tree rendering was done with TreeDyn 198.3.

div.head: Statistical Analysis
div.p: Respective values concerning earthworms and their coelomocytes were recorded individually. Results were expressed as means AE standard errors. Differences between means were determined by the Mann-Whitney U-test, with the level of significance established at P < 0.05.

div.head: Earthworm Segregation from Mixed Colony
div.p: The dense colony of composting earthworms delivered from the wastewater treatment plant in Kluczbork consisted of clitellate worms of the similar body weights (0.6-0.9 g). It was difficult to perform a morphological observation under dissecting microscope using taxonomically important features avoiding convulsive body movements (twisting) of animals connected with extrusion of yellowish coelomic fluid. Thus for the present purposes, worms were segregated according to external features into E. fetida with a distinct branding (Fig. 1A), uniformly reddish E. andrei (Fig. 1B), and more massive D. veneta (Fig. 1C).
During 5-week culture in separate boxes, body weight gain was highest in D. veneta, which reached 1.4 g, while none individual E. fetida and E. andrei exceeded 1 g body weight (Fig. 1D).

div.head: Eleocyte Autofluorescence
div.p: Flow cytometric analysis showed very distinct peaks of autofluorescence of cells with complex structure, that is, eleocytes, in all investigated specimens of the composting species. However, the intensity of eleocyte fluorescence was consistently lower in D. veneta than that in Eisenia spp. (Fig. 2).

div.head: Riboflavin
div.p: All E. andrei, E. fetida, and D. veneta possess riboflavin in coelomocyte lysates. Figure 3 shows the representative riboflavinspecific spectra obtained on coelomocyte supernatants and coelomocyte lysates of the same samples. Excitation spectra of supernatants and lysates were almost identical, exhibiting two distinct peaks at about 370 nm and 450 nm, both being lower in D. veneta than in Eisenia spp. In a sharp contrast, the emission spectra of coelomocyte supernatants were different than those of lysates. The supernatant spectra exhibited riboflavin-derived peaks at about 520-530 nm, proportional to riboflavin content, lower in D. veneta than in the both Eisenia spp. In contrast, in Triton-lysates spectra the riboflavin-derived peaks were preceded by additional emission peaks of fluorescence of the unknown origin (X fluorophore, according to Cygal et al., 2007) with a maximum of about 410-430 nm. Such X-derived peaks were especially distinct in samples from D. veneta, being in this species much higher than the riboflavin-derived peaks at 520-530 nm (Fig. 3).

Similar riboflavin and X-fluorophore spectra were obtained in supernatants and lysates of coelomocytes retrieved both from the earthworms being electrostimulated for the first time and for the second time preformed several weeks after the first expulsion, and also in the offspring of segregated animals. Albani et al. (2003) detected a species-specific fluorescence in coelomic fluid of E. andrei and stated that fluorescent properties of the emitting fluorophore are characteristic of 4-methylumbelliferyl b-D-glucuronide (MUGlcU; MUG). Under the same conditions coelomocyte lysate from individuals of E. andrei, both from Kluczbork and from Lille, exhibited spectra with MUG characteristics, with an emission peak at 370-380 nm and an excitation peak at about 310-315 nm (Fig. 4), both peaks being very clear both in cell supernatant and coelomocyte lysates. It is worth mentioning that Triton X itself exhibits fluorescence which at 1% concentration in a final solution does not interfere significantly with MUG-derived spectra (data not shown).

div.head: MUG and MUG-like Fluorophores
div.p: MUG-like fluorescence of a relatively low intensity was also present in some samples from E. fetida worms (both from Kluczbork and from Lille) with a relatively low emission peak and excitation peak shifted towards 315-320 nm but most of E. fetida samples were MUG-negative. Also all investigated specimens of D. veneta were consistently MUG-negative (Fig. 4). Similar characteristics of MUG and MUG-like spectra were obtained in lysates of coelomocytes retrieved from the earthworms being electrostimulated for the second time several weeks after the first expulsion, and also in the offspring of segregated animals.

Screening of Eisenia spp. from well established cultures in the Lille University revealed that all 54 tested specimens of E. andrei were MUG-positive and 12 of 54 tested specimens of E. fetida exhibited MUG-like fluorescence (about 22%), most E. fetida being both MUG-negative and MUG-like negative.

div.head: Nuclear DNA Content
div.p: Representative examples of propidium iodide stained DNA profiles of earthworm coelomocytes and human U937 cell line or CRBC as standards are illustrated in Figure 5. The fluorescence intensity of the G0/G1 peaks increased in order D. veneta ( E. andrei < E. fetida <<<<< U937 (Fig. 5A) and CRBC < D. veneta ( E.
andrei < E. fetida No.1 $ E. fetida No. 2 (Fig. 5B). In conclusion, among investigated earthworm species, the DNA content is consistently increasing in order D. veneta ( E. andrei < E. fetida.

div.head: DNA Barcoding of Cytochrome Oxidase Subunit I Gene (COI)
div.p: DNA sampling was performed on tail tips of earthworms being offspring of three earthworm species from Kluczbork segregated on the basis of molecular markers, that is, fluorophores and DNA amounts and from well-defined specimens of E. fetida cultured in Lille University. Phylogenetic tree based on mitochondrial COI gene shows three distinct clades corresponding with D. veneta, E. fetida, and E. andrei. All individuals of E. andrei were MUGpositive (Mp), and all D. veneta worms were MUG-negative (Mn). Most specimens of E. fetida worms were MUG-negative except 2 out 16 worms from Kluczbork (about 13%) and 7 out of 18 worms (39%) from Lille, which exhibited the presence of the MUG-like fluorophore (MLp). The presence of MLp does not correspond with two distinct subclades of E. fetida clade (Fig. 6).

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: The DNA barcoding approach proved that the dense colony of relatively small composting worms from the wastewater treatment plant consisted of the mixture of three distinct species, that is, E. andrei, E. fetida, and D. veneta. After species separation, body weight gain was significantly faster in D. veneta than in the two Eisenia species.

Coelomocyte-containing coelomic fluid, non-invasively retrievable from earthworm coelom by a mild electrostimulation, was analyzed by spectrofluorimetry and flow cytometry. Both techniques brought information supporting morphological recognition of syntopic specimens of D. veneta and Eisenia spp. Spectrofluorimetric spectra of coelomocyte lysates of D. veneta never exhibit features characteristic for MUG or MUG-like fluorophores; riboflavin content was much lower in D. veneta than that in Eisenia spp., while the peak of fluorescence derived In conclusion, these coelomocyte-derived features are very helpful in distinction of D. veneta from Eisenia spp., which is especially important in a case of juvenile specimens, but do not allow definitive distinction between E. andrei and E. fetida.

In the latter case, the most promising were fluorescence spectra present in E. andrei coelomic fluid discovered by Albani et al. (2003) fluorophore. It turned out, however, that similar spectra of fluorescence, called MUG-like in the present paper, also appeared in some specimens of E. fetida both colonies from Kluczbork and Lille. Biochemical pathways involved in MUG or MUG-like factors and their biological significance are worth undertaking detailed investigations. Nevertheless, the MUG fluorophore cannot be considered as the decisive molecular fingerprint of E. andrei only, at least in earthworm populations investigated in the present work.

Flow cytometry of propidium iodide-stained samples is among sensitive techniques for determination of nuclear DNA contents of many animal species (e.g., see Birstein et al.,'93;Tiersch et al.,'89a,b). In the present studies, the location of G0/G1 peaks of propidium iodide fluorescence indicated that the nuclear DNA content of D. veneta and Eisenia spp. coelomocytes was much lower than that of mammalian cells (i.e., U937 human cell line) but was slightly higher than that of chicken red blood cells, the latter estimated as 2.4-2.5 pg/nucleus according to Olmo ('83),and Tiersch and Wachtel ('91). A lower amount of DNA in E. fetida than that in human leukocytes and K562 cell line was previously reported by Quaglino et al. ('96). However, Vitturi et al. (2000) showed by flow cytometry assay that average diploid DNA content of E. fetida is 1.40 pg. Then Gregory and Herbert (2002) estimated the haploid genome size of E. fetida sperm/testis stained by Feulgen reaction as 0.7 pg. In both instances the nuclear DNA contents of E. fetida was much lower than that of the c one of the most chicken standard (2.5 pg). In contrast, our results suggest that the DNA content of D. veneta and Eisenia spp. coelomocytes is higher than that of chicken red blood cells. This discrepancy may be explained by the much more dispersed organization of DNA in coelomocytes versus sperm/testis nuclei, therefore further studies are necessary for establishing the nuclear DNA content of various cell types of particular earthworm species.

In the present study, the relative nuclear DNA content was always in the order Dv ( Ea < Ef, with the peaks concerning particular individuals of E. fetida being much more dispersed along the Y axis than those concerning E. andrei and D. veneta specimens. The present results concerning the lower DNA content in D. veneta than in Eisenia spp. are consistent with differences in haploid genome sizes between D. veneta versus E. fetida (0.46 and 0.7 pg, respectively) estimated by Gregory and Herbert (2002) using image-analysis densitometry of Feulgen-stained sperm and testis tissues, but it is not clear which of the two Eisenia species is being referred to. The problem of taxonomic status of E. fetida and E. andrei has been resolved quite recently, and in much of the older and even current literature both species are termed indiscriminately as E. fetida or E. foetida. In conclusion, the present results show that the propidium iodide-stained DNA diploid peaks are useful for D. veneta distinction from Eisenia spp., while peaks of E. andrei and E. fetida are less discriminatory between these species due to a wide dispersion of peaks location along the axis of fluorescence intensity in the latter species. This diversity corresponds to the presence of two subclades in the E. fetida clade obtained in the present paper by COI barcoding. Putatively, the E. fetida population from the Lille Laboratory contains a mixture of two or more sub-populations, although the founders were collected in one place.

Hybridization of the syntopic species living in mixed colonies in dung and compost heaps could be possible and such a possibility has been investigated by several authors. Dominguez et al. (2005) experimentally evidenced that there is reproductive isolation between E. fetida and E. andrei connected with postcopula isolation mechanisms; the two species mate and produce cocoons, although these cocoons did not hatch. Similar results were obtained by Reinecke and Viljoen ('91). In contrast, Andre ('63) showed that interspecific mating between E. fetida and E. andrei produced hybrid worms which were sterile and had an intermediate pigmentation pattern. Sheppard ('88) obtained fertile offspring of interspecific mating resembling the parental types, and he referred this phenomenon "facilitated self-fertilization." Mixed populations and the resulting hybridization could hamper reproduction rates if maximum yield is to be attained (Reinecke and Viljoen,'91). Presumably, the effects of hybridization in mixed populations may be dependent on the previous life history of syntopic species, thus further studies applying modern research techniques may be very fruitful.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS
div.p: Species-specific characteristics of fluorescence/molecular fingerprints of the syntopic composting species are summarized in Table 1. (1) Amount of propidium iodide stained DNA increased in order D. veneta ( E. andrei < E. fetida. (2) Intensity of eleocytederived fluorescence recorded by flow cytometry was consistently lower in D. veneta than that in Eisenia spp. (3) Amount of riboflavin recorded by spectrofluorimetry was significantly lower in coelomocyte lysates from D. veneta than from Eisenia spp. (4) The fluorescent peak (at approx. 410-420 nm) appearing in Triton X-treated coelomocyte lysates was much more distinct in D. veneta than in Eisenia spp. (5) Coelomic fluid of E. andrei exhibited specific fluorescence derived from MUG fluorophore which was lacking in D. veneta and in 75% specimens of E. fetida. (6) In the phylogenetic tree of COI gene, individuals of D. veneta, E. andrei, and E.fetida species sorted according to above-mentioned molecular markers were grouped in separate clades. Studies performed on genetically-defined E. andrei and E. fetida colonies reared in Lille University confirmed proper species segregation and the presence of the MUG-like fluorophore in all tested specimens of E. andrei and in some individuals of E. fetida.

The results of present studies inspire us to search further for non-invasively retrieved molecular markers present in composting worms and for reexamination of some aspects of their biology, like reproduction, including possibility of self-fertilization and hybridization; stress-sensitivity, including reaction to soil pollutants; ontogeny of immune system and components of coelomic fluid, including fluorophores, antibacterial and cytotoxic factors. Non-invasive methods of species identification are necessary for studies on interactions of E. andrei, E. fetida, and D. veneta cultured together.

Fluorescence spectra of emission (top) and excitation (bottom) of MUG and MUG-like fluorophore in supernatants of spanneddown samples (gray lines) and Triton-lysed samples (black lines) of coelomocytes retrieved by electrostimulation from representative specimens of Eisenia andrei MUG-positive (EaMp), Eisenia fetida MUG-like positive (EfMLp), Eisenia fetida MUG-negative (EfMn), and Dendrobaena veneta MUG-negative (DvMn).

figure.figDesc: Figure 5. DNA profiles of propidium iodide-stained samples of earthworm coelomocytes with U937 human cell line (A) or chicken red blood cells CRBC (B) used as internal standards. Representative G0/G1 peaks (from the left): (A) Dendrobaena veneta; Eisenia andrei; Eisenia fetida; U937; (B) CRBC; Dendrobaena veneta; Eisenia andrei; two specimens of Eisenia fetida.

figure.head: Figure 6 .
figure.figDesc: Figure 6. Phylogenetic tree with three distinct clades corresponding to Eisenia andrei (Ea), Eisenia fetida (Ef), and Dendrobaena veneta (Dv) earthworms being offspring of earthworms from the stock culture from Kluczbork (K) segregated on the basis of external features and molecular markers: fluorophores and DNA amounts, and specimens of E. fetida cultured in the Lille University (L). Mp, specimens MUGpositive; Mn, specimens MUG-negative; MLp, specimens MUG-like positive. Maximum likelihood tree for COI region. Genbank accession numbers for earthworms COI sequences from previous studies are indicated, full accession numbers of the worms that were sequenced in the present study are given in the Material and Methods Section. The tree is drawn to scale, with branch lengths measured in the number of substitutions per site.
